claims.text: A compositionally homogeneous high-entropy alloy with minimal short-range order can serve as the initial material state.
Sintered HfNbTaTiZr is an example of a suitable alloy for studying lattice heat conductivity.
Heat transport in the proposed HEA is contributed by both electrons and phonons.
Controlled annealing or irradiation can induce SRO precipitates in the proposed alloy.
The alloy can be studied over 50–900 °C while retaining SRO without gross phase segregation.
Processed refractory HEA structures can be useful at elevated temperatures.
SRO precipitates act as additional phonon-scattering centers.
Scattering from SRO precipitates reduces phonon scattering time.
Scattering from SRO precipitates decreases the phonon mean free path.
A reduced phonon mean free path lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
Samples containing induced SRO precipitates will have lower lattice thermal conductivity than homogeneous untreated samples.
The predicted reduction is most significant when phonons carry a large fraction of the total heat flux.
The effect may be less pronounced when electronic heat conduction dominates.
Saturation of SRO concentration beyond an optimal level may make the conductivity reduction less pronounced.
The magnitude of the conductivity reduction depends on SRO volume fraction, size, distribution, and operating temperature.
TEM or atom-probe tomography can be used to determine whether SRO precipitates are present in the treated and control samples.
Laser-flash analysis or a similar method can provide quantitative lattice thermal conductivity over 50–900 °C.
Failure to observe a statistically significant conductivity decrease, exemplified by a decrease of at least about 10%, is designated as the falsifying outcome.
